leads.name: Cèdre Gouraud
leads.status: BLOCKED 2026-09-06: dead, per the never-doe-aan-dode-bomen rule. Species is Atlas Cedar (Cedrus atlantica), estimated planted circa 1200 CE (roughly 800-900 years old at death), trunk circumference roughly 7.6m, once the largest cedar in Morocco, named for French Resident-General Henri Gouraud who was photographed beside it in April 1917. Two independent sources (lestetardsarboricoles.fr, a French tree-enthusiast site with dated field visits, and le360.ma, a Moroccan press outlet) agree it died circa 2003, likely from earthworks/soil disturbance near its roots, with the dying process lasting about three years; only the standing dead skeleton has remained since roughly 2006, leafless for over a decade per le360.ma's own more recent (undated but clearly post-2010s) revisit piece. No living replacement planting at the same spot is documented anywhere. It remains a popular tourist stop (~60,000 visitors/year) purely as a dead monument/curiosity, which is exactly the case the rule excludes: 'a carcass, stump or relic breaks the promise and makes the years-counter lie... a dead tree may appear inside a story as context, never as a collectible entry, however famous the remains.' Unlike the Elm of Saint-Gervais precedent, there is no living successor tree to publish instead. NOT a candidate to ship. Worth noting for a future pass: multiple sources describe Azrou's wider cedar forest (la cedraie d'Azrou) as containing other genuinely ancient LIVING cedars nearby (some sources loosely claim 'cedres millenaires'), which could be a separate, real candidate if a specific living specimen with its own coordinates and sourcing can be identified; that research was not done this pass since the brief's candidate was specifically the Gouraud tree.
